- When sentiment is strongly positive (≥ 0.8) in recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly to avoid overshoot.
- When sentiment is strongly negative (≤ -0.2) or volatile, model often underestimates; adjust upward to reflect risk aversion or market panic.
- Model consistently overpredicts early in the 30-day horizon (especially days 1–5) when sentiment is neutral or mildly positive — apply downward bias for first 5 days.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 70), model often overcorrects or fails to sustain momentum — reduce forecast by 1–2% for next 3–5 days to reflect mean reversion.
- If sentiment history shows repeated short-term reversals (e.g., +0.4 → -0.2 → +0.6), model tends to lag — adjust forecast 1–2 days ahead to align with sentiment momentum.
- When sentiment is flat or low (0.2–0.4), model often underperforms — increase forecast by 0.5–1.5% to compensate for low conviction.
- Avoid forecasting “flat” or “no change” when sentiment shows clear direction — even if price is stable, sentiment implies directional bias.
